message_source_quote: Built from independently authored prompts with different concepts, carriers, and instruction wordings than the WBS paper's `directed_modulation` items — testing and confirming that the stance direction transfers across prompt sets.
writeup_source_quote: This mirrors the white-bear stance contrast of Raman et al. (2026), but from prompts I authored — not WorkspaceBench's `directed_modulation` items.

differences.writeup_quote: This mirrors the white-bear stance contrast of Raman et al. (2026)
differences.what: The write-up explicitly names the source as Raman et al. (2026) and calls it the 'white-bear stance contrast'; the message only refers to it obliquely as 'the WBS paper', never naming the authors or the 'white-bear' term, giving a vaguer identification of the source even though both describe the same overlap (directed_modulation items) and the same novelty claim (independently authored prompts transferring the stance).

rationale: The write-up explicitly credits Raman et al. (2026) and the 'white-bear stance contrast' as the basis the method mirrors, built instead from self-authored prompts rather than WorkspaceBench's directed_modulation items, and frames novelty as testing whether the stance transfers to a different prompt set. The message makes the same substantive novelty claim (self-authored prompts outperforming the directed_modulation reproduction, testing transfer of the stance direction) but only refers to the source obliquely as 'the WBS paper' without naming the authors or the white-bear concept, so it conveys the same overlap/novelty content with less explicit sourcing than the write-up, and contains no statements about the write-up document itself to check for falsity.
